claim: Staphylococcus aureus is estimated to colonize between 20–50% of the healthy human population.
source: Staphylococcus aureus is a commensal bacterium that is estimated to colonize between 20–50% of the healthy human population (Naimi et al., 2003; Graham et al., 2006; Enright et al., 2002; Ohara-Nemoto et al., 2008; Zafar et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: S. aureus colonization typically occurs in the nares, throat, or on the skin.
source: Colonization typically occurs in the nares, throat, or on the skin (Ohara-Nemoto et al., 2008; Zafar et al., 2007; Hamdan-Partida et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The dominant fraction of invasive S. aureus infections occur in the context of bacteremia.
source: The dominant fraction of invasive infections caused by this bacterium occur in the context of bacteremia (Klevens et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Klevens et al., 2007.

claim: Pneumonia and septic shock caused by S. aureus have mortality rates in the United States of 30–55%.
source: In the United States, pneumonia and septic shock are rapidly progressing infections and are often fatal with mortality rates in the United States (US) of 30–55% (Klevens et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Klevens et al., 2007.

claim: Nearly 92% of invasive S. aureus infection cases in the US required hospitalization.
source: A recent epidemiological analysis of ~8,700 cases of invasive S. aureus infections in the US found that nearly 92% cases required hospitalization (Klevens et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to an epidemiological analysis.

claim: USA300 methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) has emerged as the dominant etiologic agent of community-associated invasive infections in the United States.
source: In the United States, pulsed-field type USA300 methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) has emerged as the dominant etiologic agent of community-associated invasive infections (Klevens et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Klevens et al., 2007.

claim: S. aureus strains have been isolated that are resistant to nearly all clinically available antibiotics, including linezolid and daptomycin.
source: S. aureus strains have been isolated that are resistant to nearly all clinically available antibiotics, including the last-line antibiotics linezolid and daptomycin (Sass et al., 2012; Sánchez García et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Approximately 99% of bacteria establish biofilms in their natural environments.
source: It has been theorized, based upon studies using direct techniques, such as microscopy, that ~99% of bacteria establish biofilms in their natural environments (Costerton et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and is described as a theory based on microscopy studies.

claim: Biofilms are considered to be the etiologic agents of recurrent staphylococcal infections.
source: Reflective of their clinical significance, biofilms are considered to be the etiologic agents of recurrent staphylococcal infections (Joo and Otto, 2012; Otto, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: S. aureus biofilms are typically composed of one or more extracellular polymeric molecules (DNA, proteins, or polysaccharides).
source: S. aureus biofilms are typically composed of one or more extracellular polymeric molecules (DNA, proteins, or polysaccharides) that provide structural integrity and may also facilitate intercellular adhesion (Rice et al., 2007; Schwartz et al., 2012; Boles and Horswill, 2008; Cramton et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Oxygen concentrations vary greatly between healthy human tissues (between 19.7 to ~1.5%).
source: Oxygen concentrations vary greatly between healthy human tissues (between 19.7 to ~1.5%; normoxia) (Carreau et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Carreau et al., 2011.

claim: Oxygen concentrations in infected or necrotic tissues and wounds are estimated to be below 1% (hypoxic) or anoxic.
source: Oxygen concentrations also vary between healthy and infected or necrotic tissues, as well as in wounds, where concentrations are estimated to be below 1% (hypoxic) or anoxic (Carreau et al., 2011; Vogelberg and König, 1993; Arnold et al., 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: S. aureus infections in skeletal tissues (osteomyelitis) cause an approximately 3-fold decrease in oxygen concentrations.
source: A recent study found that S. aureus infections in skeletal tissues (osteomyelitis) cause an ~3 fold decrease in oxygen concentrations resulting in increasing hypoxia as infection proceeds (Wilde et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wilde et al., 2015.

claim: Decreased oxygen concentrations result in increased biofilm formation in S. aureus.
source: A study by Cramton et al. found that decreased oxygen concentrations result in increased biofilm formation in S. aureus (Cramton et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cramton et al., 2001.

claim: S. aureus growing in biofilms are starved for oxygen and the rate of oxygen depletion is proportional to the rate of biofilm maturation.
source: An alternate study found that S. aureus growing in biofilms are starved for oxygen and that the rate of oxygen depletion is proportional to the rate of biofilm maturation (Zhu et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhu et al., 2007.

claim: Biofilm formation increased substantially for each S. aureus strain (LAC, SH1000, MW2, N315) during anaerobic growth (between ~4–30 fold).
source: Biofilm formation increased substantially for each strain during anaerobic growth (between ~4–30 fold) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Oxygen influences biofilm formation in its capacity as a terminal electron acceptor for cellular respiration.
source: Data presented show that oxygen impacts biofilm formation in its capacity as a terminal electron acceptor in cellular respiration.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and logical inference from the results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Anaerobic biofilm formation decreased as the concentration of nitrate provided in the medium was increased.
source: Anaerobic biofilm formation decreased, as the concentration of nitrate provided in the medium was increased (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A hemB::Tn strain formed considerably more biofilm than the WT when cultured aerobically.
source: A hemB::Tn strain formed considerably more biofilm than the WT when cultured aerobically, but displayed biofilm formation similar to the WT when cultured fermentatively (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Nitrate supplementation did not decrease anaerobic biofilm formation in a nitrate reductase (narG::Tn) mutant.
source: Likewise, nitrate supplementation did not decrease anaerobic biofilm formation in a nitrate reductase (narG::Tn) mutant, which is unable to utilize nitrate as a TEA (Figure 1E) (Schlag et al., 2008; Burke and Lascelles, 1975).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and citations.

claim: Biofilm formation increased in synchrony with the concentration of sodium azide in the growth medium.
source: Biofilm formation increased in synchrony with the concentration of sodium azide in the growth medium (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Decreased cellular respiration results in increased biofilm formation.
source: From Figure 1 we concluded that decreased cellular respiration results in increased biofilm formation.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Biofilm formation was responsive to the concentration of a terminal electron acceptor or the ability of cells to respire.
source: Further, biofilm formation was responsive to the concentration of a terminal electron acceptor or the ability of cells to respire.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Strains lacking functional IcaA, IcaB, or IcaC were not attenuated in fermentative biofilm formation.
source: Strains lacking functional IcaA, IcaB, or IcaC were not attenuated in fermentative biofilm formation, suggesting that PIA is dispensable for this phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Supplementation of the growth medium with DNase substantially attenuated biofilm formation.
source: However, supplementation of the growth medium with DNase, which degrades DNA, substantially attenuated biofilm formation suggesting that DNA is an integral component of fermentative biofilms (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The accumulation of high-molecular weight extracellular DNA (eDNA) increased appreciably in the matrix of fermenting biofilms.
source: Consistent with this theory, the accumulation of high-molecular weight extracellular DNA (eDNA) increased appreciably in the matrix of fermenting biofilms (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A strain lacking the atlA::Tn was attenuated in fermentative biofilm formation.
source: One strain, with a disruption in the gene encoding for the AtlA murein hydrolase (atlA::Tn), was attenuated in biofilm formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The atlA::Tn strain displayed decreased biofilm formation in the presence of oxygen (~1 fold decrease) and this phenotype was exacerbated (~10 fold decrease) in fermenting cultures.
source: The atlA::Tn strain displayed decreased biofilm formation in the presence of oxygen (~1 fold decrease) and this phenotype was exacerbated (~10 fold decrease) in fermenting cultures (Figure 2C) suggesting that the role of AtlA in biofilm formation is increased during fermentative growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: eDNA accumulation was greatly decreased in the biofilm matrix of the fermentatively cultured atlA::Tn strain.
source: Moreover, eDNA accumulation was greatly decreased in the biofilm matrix of the fermentatively cultured atlA::Tn strain (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Supplementation of media with proteinase K attenuated fermentative biofilm formation.
source: The supplementation of media with proteinase K, which degrades proteins, attenuated fermentative biofilm formation, suggesting that in addition to eDNA, proteins also form an integral part of the biofilm matrix in fermenting cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The spent media supernatant from fermenting WT had ~5 fold increased Kat activity relative to aerobically cultured WT.
source: The spent media supernatant from fermenting WT had ~5 fold increased Kat activity relative to aerobically cultured WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Kat activity was decreased by ~5 fold in the spent media supernatant from the fermentatively cultured altA::Tn strain.
source: Kat activity was decreased by ~5 fold in the spent media supernatant from the fermentatively cultured altA::Tn strain (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Fermenting cells release an increased quantity of DNA and cytoplasmic proteins into their extracellular mileu in an AtlA-dependent manner.
source: From Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–4 we concluded that fermenting cells release an increased quantity of DNA and cytoplasmic proteins, into their extracellular mileu, in an AtlA-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 2 and its supplements.

claim: The atlA transcript was increased ~5 fold upon fermentative culture.
source: The atlA transcript was increased ~5 fold upon fermentative culture (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Fermentatively cultured WT cells underwent autolysis faster than those cultured aerobically.
source: Fermentatively cultured WT cells underwent autolysis faster than those cultured aerobically.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from autolysis assays.

claim: The atlA::Tn strain, cultured aerobically or fermentatively, was severely deficient in undergoing autolysis.
source: The atlA::Tn strain, cultured aerobically or fermentatively, was severely deficient in undergoing autolysis suggesting that AtlA was the dominant murein hydrolase contributing to autolysis under the growth conditions examined (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CW-extracts from fermenting WT lysed M. luteus more rapidly than CW-extracts from WT cultured aerobically.
source: CW-extracts from fermenting WT lysed M. luteus more rapidly than CW-extracts from WT cultured aerobically (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CW-extracts from the ΔatlA strain carrying patlA or patlAAM lysed fermentatively cultured heat-killed WT at a faster rate than aerobically cultured WT.
source: CW-extracts from the ΔatlA strain carrying patlA or patlAAM lysed fermentatively cultured heat-killed WT at a faster rate than aerobically cultured WT, suggesting fermenting S. aureus cells are more amenable to cleavage by AtlA and AM (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: The transcription of genes encoding for proteins in the WTA biosynthetic pathway (tarA, tarO, tarB, tarH) was decreased during fermentative growth (between 6–50 fold).
source: Consistent with this logic, the transcription of genes encoding for proteins in the WTA biosynthetic pathway (tarA, tarO, tarB, tarH) was decreased during fermentative growth (between 6–50 fold) (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The influence of pH upon AtlA activity, in both murein hydrolase and autolysis assays, was almost entirely as a result of alterations in WTA expression.
source: We found that the influence of pH upon AtlA activity, in both murein hydrolase, as well as autolysis assays, was almost entirely as a result of alterations in WTA expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from murein hydrolase and autolysis assays.

claim: Tunicamycin treated cells bound a majority of the bacteriolytic activity corresponding to AtlA at pH 5.
source: We found that at a pH of 5, tunicamycin treated cells bound a majority of the bacteriolytic activity corresponding to AtlA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from binding assays.

claim: Aerobically or fermentatively cultured heat-killed WT cells did not bind bacteriolytic enzymes at pH 5.
source: In contrast, binding was absent in cells not treated with tunicamycin, regardless of whether they were cultured aerobically or fermentatively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from binding assays.

claim: Fermenting S. aureus had increased expression of AtlA and concomitantly decreased expression of wall-teichoic acids.
source: From Figures 3, 4, and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2, we concluded that fermenting S. aureus had increased expression of AtlA and concomitantly decreased expression of wall-teichoic acids.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Impaired respiration elicits programmed cell lysis (PCL).
source: Since the changes in expression were accompanied by similar changes in transcription we concluded that impaired respiration elicits programmed cell lysis (PCL).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing transcriptional changes.

claim: A strain lacking the staphylococcal respiratory regulatory system (SrrAB) was attenuated in fermentative biofilm formation.
source: A strain lacking the staphylococcal respiratory regulatory system (SrrAB) was attenuated in fermentative biofilm formation (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Reintroduction of srrAB into the ΔsrrAB strain upon an episome restored fermentative biofilm formation.
source: Reintroduction of srrAB into the ΔsrrAB strain upon an episome restored fermentative biofilm formation (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The introduction of a ΔsrrAB mutation into a hemB::Tn strain attenuated the increased biofilm formation of the hemB::Tn strain during aerobic growth.
source: Consistent with SrrAB mediated changes in biofilm formation occurring as a result of altered respiratory status, the introduction of a ΔsrrAB mutation into a hemB::Tn strain attenuated the increased biofilm formation of the hemB::Tn strain during aerobic growth (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The abundance of the atlA transcript was decreased (~5 fold) in the ΔsrrAB strain.
source: The abundance of the atlA transcript was decreased (~5 fold) in the ΔsrrAB strain (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The abundances of transcripts corresponding to genes required for WTA biosynthesis were increased in the ΔsrrAB strain (~2.5–5 fold).
source: In contrast, the abundances of transcripts corresponding to genes required for WTA biosynthesis were increased in the ΔsrrAB strain (~2.5–5 fold).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR assays.

claim: The fermentative biofilm formation phenotype of the ΔsrrAB atlA::Tn strain was similar to that of the atlA::Tn strain.
source: The fermentative biofilm formation phenotype of the ΔsrrAB atlA::Tn strain was similar to that of the atlA::Tn strain, suggesting that SrrAB influences biofilm formation, in part, via AtlA (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The ΔsrrAB strain was deficient in autolysis.
source: Moreover, the ΔsrrAB strain was deficient in autolysis (Figure 5E) and had decreased accumulation of eDNA in its biofilm matrix when cultured fermentatively (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The ΔsrrAB strain had decreased accumulation of eDNA in its biofilm matrix when cultured fermentatively.
source: Moreover, the ΔsrrAB strain was deficient in autolysis (Figure 5E) and had decreased accumulation of eDNA in its biofilm matrix when cultured fermentatively (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The presence of patlA partially suppressed the fermentative biofilm formation defect of the ΔsrrAB strain when compared to the strain carrying patlAAM H263A.
source: The presence of patlA partially suppressed the fermentative biofilm formation defect of the ΔsrrAB strain when compared to the strain carrying patlAAM H263A (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Fermentatively cultured, heat-killed, ΔsrrAB cells were lysed at a slower rate by CW-extracts from the ΔatlA strain carrying patlA.
source: Additionally, fermentatively cultured, heat-killed, ΔsrrAB cells were lysed at a slower rate by CW-extracts from the ΔatlA strain carrying patlA, consistent with increased expression of WTA in the ΔsrrAB strain (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The transcription of genes positively regulated by SrrAB were reduced in a menaquinone auxotroph.
source: Upon analyzing previous studies we observed that the transcription of genes positively regulated by SrrAB were reduced in a menaquinone auxotroph (Kohler et al., 2008; Kinkel et al., 2013; Yarwood et al., 2001; Pragman et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The hemB::Tn strain, ΔsrrAB hemB::Tn, hemB::Tn menF:Tn, and ΔsrrAB hemB::Tn menF::Tn strains phenocopied the biofilm formation of the menF::Tn strain.
source: Importantly, the ΔsrrAB hemB::Tn, hemB::Tn menF:Tn, and ΔsrrAB hemB::Tn menF::Tn strains phenocopied the biofilm formation of the menF::Tn strain (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The presence of menaquinone is necessary for SrrAB-dependent biofilm formation in a hemB::Tn strain.
source: These data confirmed that the presence of menaquinone is necessary for SrrAB-dependent biofilm formation in a hemB::Tn strain.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: The ΔndhC ndhF::Tn sdh:Tn strain displayed a negligible increase in aerobic biofilm formation (~1.4 fold increase).
source: The ΔndhC ndhF::Tn sdh:Tn strain displayed a negligible increase in aerobic biofilm formation (~1.4 fold increase), which was phenocopied by the ΔsrrAB ΔndhC ndhF::Tn sdh:Tn strain (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Menaquinone influences SrrAB activity with respect to biofilm formation.
source: Taken together, the data in Figure 6 led us to infer that with respect to biofilm formation (1) menaquinone influences SrrAB activity, (2) the absence of menaquinone results in SrrAB being non-responsive, (3) SrrAB activity is increased upon enrichment of reduced menaquinone, and (4) SrrAB is non-responsive to the enrichment of oxidized menaquinone.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The absence of menaquinone results in SrrAB being non-responsive with respect to biofilm formation.
source: Taken together, the data in Figure 6 led us to infer that with respect to biofilm formation (1) menaquinone influences SrrAB activity, (2) the absence of menaquinone results in SrrAB being non-responsive, (3) SrrAB activity is increased upon enrichment of reduced menaquinone, and (4) SrrAB is non-responsive to the enrichment of oxidized menaquinone.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: SrrAB activity is increased upon enrichment of reduced menaquinone with respect to biofilm formation.
source: Taken together, the data in Figure 6 led us to infer that with respect to biofilm formation (1) menaquinone influences SrrAB activity, (2) the absence of menaquinone results in SrrAB being non-responsive, (3) SrrAB activity is increased upon enrichment of reduced menaquinone, and (4) SrrAB is non-responsive to the enrichment of oxidized menaquinone.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: SrrAB is non-responsive to the enrichment of oxidized menaquinone with respect to biofilm formation.
source: Taken together, the data in Figure 6 led us to infer that with respect to biofilm formation (1) menaquinone influences SrrAB activity, (2) the absence of menaquinone results in SrrAB being non-responsive, (3) SrrAB activity is increased upon enrichment of reduced menaquinone, and (4) SrrAB is non-responsive to the enrichment of oxidized menaquinone.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Impaired respiration leads to increased cell lysis via divergent regulation of two processes: increased expression of the AtlA murein hydrolase and decreased expression of wall-teichoic acids.
source: Impaired respiration led to increased cell lysis via divergent regulation of two processes: increased expression of the AtlA murein hydrolase and decreased expression of wall-teichoic acids.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing transcriptional changes and phenotypic effects.

claim: The AltA-dependent release of cytosolic DNA contributed to increased biofilm formation.
source: The AltA-dependent release of cytosolic DNA contributed to increased biofilm formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing eDNA accumulation and biofilm formation phenotypes.

claim: Cell lysis and biofilm formation were governed by the SrrAB two-component regulatory system.
source: Further, cell lysis and biofilm formation were governed by the SrrAB two-component regulatory system.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing phenotypes of SrrAB mutants.

claim: SrrAB-dependent biofilm formation occurs in response to the accumulation of reduced menaquinone.
source: Data presented support a model wherein SrrAB-dependent biofilm formation occurs in response to the accumulation of reduced menaquinone.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic evidence from experiments with menaquinone mutants.

claim: Biofilms provide protection from environmental stress, innate immunity, as well as therapeutic agents.
source: This matrix provides protection from environmental stress, innate immunity, as well as therapeutic agents (Davies, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Davies, 2003.

claim: S. aureus can utilize nitrate as a terminal electron acceptor in addition to oxygen.
source: In addition to oxygen, S. aureus can utilize nitrate as a TEA.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about S. aureus metabolism.

claim: Heme auxotrophs have non-functional terminal oxidases and are unable to respire.
source: Heme auxotrophs have non-functional terminal oxidases and are unable to respire.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about heme auxotrophs and is supported by citations.

claim: Small-colony variants form small colonies when cultured in the presence of oxygen.
source: They, form small colonies when cultured in the presence of oxygen, and therefore are termed small-colony variants (Hammer et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hammer et al., 2013.

claim: AtlA has been previously implicated to be required for biofilm formation during aerobic growth.
source: AtlA has been previously implicated to be required for biofilm formation during aerobic growth (Bose et al., 2012; Houston et al., 2011; Biswas et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: AtlA has been implicated in the release of cytosolic proteins into the extracellular milleu.
source: AtlA has been implicated in the release of cytosolic proteins into the extracellular milleu (Pasztor et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pasztor et al., 2010.

claim: Wall-teichoic acids (WTA) negatively modulate AtlA activity.
source: Wall-teichoic acids (WTA) are cell-surface glycopolymers that are covalently attached to peptidoglycan. The biosynthetic pathway for WTA in S. aureus is illustrated in Figure 4A. WTA negatively modulate AtlA activity (Biswas et al., 2012; Schlag et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Biswas et al., 2012 and Schlag et al., 2010.

claim: Tunicamycin inhibits TarO and MnaA, which are necessary for WTA biosynthesis.
source: Tunicamycin is an inhibitor of TarO and MnaA, which are necessary for WTA biosynthesis (Figure 4A) (Campbell et al., 2011; Mann et al., 2016; Hancock et al., 1976).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: S. aureus cultured in the presence of tunicamycin do not synthesize WTA.
source: S. aureus cultured in the presence of tunicamycin do not synthesize WTA (Campbell et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Campbell et al., 2011.

claim: Schlag et al. found that the presence of WTA interferes with the binding of AtlA to the cell surface.
source: Schlag et al. found that the presence of WTA interferes with the binding of AtlA to the cell surface (Schlag et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schlag et al., 2010.

claim: Biswas et al. found that WTA contributes to proton binding on the cell surface.
source: Biswas et al. found that WTA contributes to proton binding on the cell surface.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Biswas et al., 2012.

claim: AtlA activity decreases substantially below pH 6.5.
source: AtlA activity decreases substantially below pH 6.5 (Biswas et al., 2012), and therefore, it was proposed that binding of protons by WTA leads to a decrease in the local pH of the cell surface thereby inhibiting AtlA activity (Biswas et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Biswas et al., 2012.

claim: The complete loss of WTA expression increases binding of AtlA to the cell surface.
source: We concluded that the complete loss of WTA expression does indeed increase binding of AtlA to the cell surface confirming and extending the findings of Schlag et al. (2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from binding assays and extends previous findings.

claim: Altered AtlA binding to WTA was unlikely to underlie the increased lysis of fermenting cells.
source: However, altered AtlA binding to WTA was unlikely to underlie the increased lysis of fermenting cells.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing no difference in binding between aerobic and fermentative cells.

claim: The combination of increased expression of AtlA and decreased expression of wall-teichoic acids facilitates increased autolysis.
source: The combination of these two divergent responses facilitates increased autolysis.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing divergent regulation.

claim: SrrAB influences PCL and biofilm formation by divergently influencing AtlA and WTA expression.
source: These data suggest that SrrAB influences PCL and biofilm formation by divergently influencing AtlA and WTA expression.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing transcriptional changes in SrrAB mutants.

claim: SrrAB output was previously shown to be altered under conditions of hypoxia and nitric oxide stress.
source: SrrAB output was previously shown to be altered under conditions of hypoxia and nitric oxide stress (Kinkel et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kinkel et al., 2013.

claim: The cellular molecule(s) that influence SrrAB activity are unidentified.
source: However, the cellular molecule(s) that influence SrrAB activity are unidentified.
evidence: The claim is based on the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: S. aureus synthesizes menaquinone and strains lacking menaquinone are unable to respire.
source: S. aureus synthesizes menaquinone and strains lacking menaquinone are unable to respire (Wakeman et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wakeman et al., 2012.

claim: Heme and menaquinone auxotrophs are both deficient in respiration and the concentration of fermentative by-products and the pH in the spent media is similar in these strains.
source: However, heme and menaquinone auxotrophs are both deficient in respiration and the concentration of fermentative by-products and the pH in the spent media is similar in these strains ((Hammer et al., 2013) and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and unpublished data.

claim: Heme and menaquinone auxotrophs display a similar decrease in membrane potential.
source: These strains also display a similar decrease in membrane potential (Hammer et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hammer et al., 2013.

claim: Only a heme auxotroph forms SrrAB-dependent biofilms among respiratory-deficient strains.
source: Yet, only a heme auxotroph forms SrrAB-dependent biofilms.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing heme and menaquinone auxotrophs.

claim: It is unlikely that pH or alterations in proton motive force alter SrrAB activity with respect to biofilm formation.
source: Thus, we deem it unlikely that pH or alterations in proton motive force alter SrrAB activity with respect to biofilm formation.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing heme and menaquinone auxotrophs.

claim: ArcB is proposed to donate electrons from conserved cysteine residues to oxidized quinones resulting in silencing of kinase activity.
source: ArcB is proposed to donate electrons from conserved cysteine residues to oxidized quinones resulting in silencing of kinase activity (Malpica et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Malpica et al., 2004.

claim: SrrB contains three conserved cysteine residues, which may facilitate redox interactions with the menaquinone pool.
source: Similar to ArcB, SrrB contains three conserved cysteine residues, which may facilitate redox interactions with the menaquinone pool.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis and speculation about potential function.

claim: The molecular mechanism of SrrB signaling may be similar to ArcB.
source: While this leads to the supposition that the molecular mechanism of SrrB signaling may be similar to ArcB, further biochemical analyses are required to make this conclusion.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on similarities between SrrB and ArcB.

claim: B. subtilis increases biofilm formation under hypoxic growth and this phenotype is reversed upon supplementation with the alternate TEA nitrate.
source: Similar to S. aureus, B. subtilis increases biofilm formation under hypoxic growth and this phenotype is reversed upon supplementation with the alternate TEA nitrate (Kolodkin-Gal et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kolodkin-Gal et al., 2013.

claim: Biofilm formation in B. subtilis coincided with increased transcription of genes required for matrix production, which was mediated via the membrane-associated kinases KinA and KinB.

claim: P. aeruginosa increases biofilm formation under hypoxic growth and this phenotype is reversed upon supplementation with the alternate TEA nitrate.

claim: Clinical isolates of S. aureus that are incapable of respiration, termed as small colony variants (SCV), display increased resistance towards antibiotics and cause persistent infections.

claim: The SCV phenotype often arises as a result of mutations in genes necessary for heme biosynthesis resulting in non-functional terminal oxidases.

claim: A heme auxotroph forms SrrAB-dependent biofilms, which lends insight into the mechanisms that may predominate within clinical SCV strains.

source: Similar to PCD, the findings presented herein suggest that PCL may provide bacteria with a population-level advantage by facilitating biofilm establishment, thereby imparting protection from the immune system and therapeutic agents.

claim: Hypoxia triggered PCD manifests as a mixture of apoptosis and necrosis.

claim: Anoxia triggered PCD is largely an apoptotic process.
